15.t: Working with data: a fish stock
q: Calculate the catch as a percentage of the breeding stock in 1970 and in 1990.
Identify when harvesting became unsustainable. Explain.
From about 1970–1980: the stock fell every year while the catch was kept up or increased, so more was taken than reproduction could replace.
Explain why the catch stayed high while the stock fell.
More boats and better technology (sonar, bigger nets) let fishers keep catching as fish became scarcer.
Fishing nearly stopped in 1995, yet the stock barely recovered by 2010. Suggest two reasons.
Any two: very few breeding adults left; the fish mature slowly; the ecosystem changed (more predators or competitors); fish still caught as bycatch.
Suggest two measures that keep a fishery sustainable.
Any two: catch quotas below the maximum sustainable yield; minimum net mesh sizes; closed seasons or areas; marine reserves.
Describe the changes in dissolved oxygen downstream of the drain.
Oxygen falls sharply from 9.5 to about 3.5 mg dm⁻³ at 1 km, then recovers to 8.8 by 5 km.
Explain the low oxygen just below the drain.
The drain adds organic matter and fertiliser (eutrophication). Decomposers (bacteria) multiply and respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen: shown by the high BOD.
Explain the recovery further downstream.
The organic matter is broken down or diluted, so BOD falls; oxygen dissolves from the air and is released by photosynthesis.
Explain why mayfly nymphs are useful indicator species here.
They need high oxygen, so their absence shows pollution and their return shows recovery, without chemical tests.
Suggest why BOD at 5 km is still above the upstream value.
Some organic matter from the drain is still being decomposed.

24.t: Working with data: mercury in a food chain
q: Calculate how many times higher the mercury concentration is in the bird than in algae.
Calculate the concentration factor from water to algae.
Explain why mercury concentration increases along the food chain.
Mercury is not broken down or excreted; it is stored in the body. Each consumer eats many organisms from the level below over its life, so mercury builds up at each level: biomagnification.
The pike is just under the safe limit. Suggest advice for people who fish here.
Eat large predatory fish rarely (especially pregnant women and young children); choose small fish; older, larger pike will have more.
Explain why top predators are worst affected, even though algae take mercury in directly.
They are at the top of the biomagnification chain and are long-lived, so they keep accumulating mercury for years.
